sec.title: Background
sec.p: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) have been shown to reduce cardiovascular risk, but direct comparison is limited. Objective: Compare the effects of SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonist on major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in adults with T2DM using randomized controlled trials and indirect comparisons.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, CENTRAL, and Google Scholar was conducted through October 20, 2025, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251168485). We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of SGLT2i or GLP-1RA versus placebo in adults with T2DM that reported cardiovascular or renal outcomes. Pooled hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using the generic inverse variance method with a random-effects model. An indirect treatment comparison was performed using the Bucher method. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane RoB 1 tool.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We reviewed twelve trials involving 99,261 individuals (5 SGLT2i, 7 GLP-1RA). Compared to placebo, SGLT2i significantly reduced MACE (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.84–0.95; p = 0.0003), as did GLP-1RA (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.78–0.87; p < 0.00001). The indirect comparison indicated a nominally greater MACE reduction with GLP-1RA (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.00–1.18; p = 0.0497). SGLT2i demonstrated pronounced benefits for heart failure hospitalization (HR 0.68) and composite renal outcomes (HR 0.69), while GLP-1RA showed significant but more modest effects on these endpoints and greater benefits for atherosclerotic events and weight loss.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Both SGLT2i and GLP-1RA are highly effective in reducing MACE in high-risk T2DM. Their markedly different secondary outcome profiles for heart failure, renal protection, atherosclerotic events, and weight loss underscore that they are complementary rather than interchangeable. The optimal choice should be individualized based on the patient's predominant comorbidities, treatment goals, and local access.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the principal cause of morbidity and mortality in individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), accounting for nearly half of the deaths in this population [1]. The mechanisms by which diabetes leads to cardiovascular disease include chronic hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and low-grade inflammation which all contribute to accelerated atherosclerosis and cardiac remodeling [2].

In the past decade, two classes of glucose-lowering agents—sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA)—have changed the management of T2DM; these drugs provide benefits beyond glycemic control. Trials with large sample sizes as randomized controlled trials (RCTs), have demonstrated that both drug classes reduce major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), heart failure hospitalizations, and improve renal outcomes in high-risk patients with diabetes [3–14].

SGLT2 inhibitors mainly promote glucosuria, natriuresis, and osmotic diuresis which decrease plasma volume, preload and afterload, leading to improved cardiac and renal function [15, 16]. GLP-1 receptor agonists have cardioprotective effects via metabolic and anti atherogenic pathways that lead to improved endothelial function, blood pressure, and lipid metabolism, as well as decreased inflammation and body weight [17, 18]. Recent reviews emphasize GLP-1RA’s role in obesity management, which may amplify CV benefits in T2DM patients with comorbid overweight [19].

While both classes provide cardiovascular benefits, it remains unclear whether SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists provide superior cardiovascular protection. Prior meta-analyses have yielded confusing results with some reporting a greater reduction in heart failure with SGLT2 inhibitors and others reporting a more robust reduction in MACE with GLP-1 receptor agonists [15–21]. Therefore, the purpose of this meta-analysis was to conduct a systematic review to directly compare cardiovascular outcomes with SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists in adults with T2DM using data from placebo-controlled randomized trials and indirect comparisons between the two classes.

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: A systematic search of the literature was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) and Google Scholar from inception to October 20, 2025, in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The protocol for this systematic review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251168485).

The search included the following combinations of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH): “SGLT2 inhibitors,” “GLP-1 receptor agonists,” “type 2 diabetes,” “cardiovascular outcomes,” and “major adverse cardiovascular events.” Specific drug names were also searched (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, ertugliflozin, liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide, efpeglenatide, albiglutide). Studies were limited to those involving humans, published in English, and including participants aged ≥ 18 years. The reference lists of the articles and reviews included were reviewed to identify studies which might be eligible. The study selection process is outlined in the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram (Fig. 1). The detailed search strategy for all databases is provided in Additional File 2.

caption.p: Prisma flow diagram

sec.title: Eligibility criteria
sec.p: Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adult patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus who received either an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1 receptor agonist compared to placebo. Trials were required to report at least one of the following cardiovascular or renal outcomes:

list-item.p: Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).
Hospitalization for heart failure (HHF).
Cardiovascular death.
Composite renal outcomes.
All-cause mortality.

sec.p: Studies were excluded if they were non-randomized, observational, lacked cardiovascular endpoints, or had a follow-up shorter than 12 weeks.

Trials with primary renal endpoints (e.g., CREDENCE, FLOW) were included as they reported pre-specified adjudicated cardiovascular outcomes as key secondary endpoints, and their populations remain at high cardiovascular risk. The AMPLITUDE-O trial, which enrolled patients with very high-risk profiles, was included to ensure our analysis captures the full spectrum of treatment effects across risk strata, reflecting real-world clinical diversity.

sec.title: Data extraction and management
sec.p: Two independent reviewers (A.A.O.A. and O.A.O.A.) extracted data from each eligible trial using a standardized data extraction form. A third reviewer (Ra.A.O.A.) was available to resolve any discrepancies through discussion and consensus. The extracted data included:

list-item.p: Study characteristics (author, year, trial title).
Details about the intervention and comparator.
Sample size and population characteristics.
Duration of follow-up.
Outcomes reported (HRs with 95% CIs).

sec.p: The characteristics of the included trials are summarized in (Table 1). All extracted data were verified against the original publications for accuracy, and the complete data extraction sheet is available as a supplementary file (see Additional File 1).

caption.p: Characteristics of included randomized controlled trials

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: The methodological quality of the included randomized controlled trials was independently assessed by two reviewers using the Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB 1) tool described in the Cochrane Handbook. This included seven domains: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other bias.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using Review Manager (RevMan) version 5.4. Pooled hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using the generic inverse variance method with a random-effects model. Separate pairwise meta-analyses were conducted for:

list-item.p: SGLT2 inhibitors versus placebo.
GLP-1 receptor agonists versus placebo.

sec.p: An indirect treatment comparison between the two drug classes was then performed using the Bucher method, which compares pooled treatment effects from the separate pairwise meta-analyses, provided there is a common comparator (placebo).

Heterogeneity across trials was assessed using Cochran’s Q (χ²) test and quantified by the I² statistic. I² values < 25%, 25–50%, and > 75% were interpreted as indicating low, moderate, and substantial heterogeneity, respectively. The statistical significance level was set at p < 0.05 (two-tailed).

To assess the robustness of the primary MACE findings, we performed pre-specified sensitivity analyses by sequentially excluding trials with specific design features: the trial with a primary renal endpoint (CREDENCE) from the SGLT2i analysis, and the trial with a uniquely high-risk population (AMPLITUDE-O) from the GLP-1RA analysis. The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations) framework.

sec.title: Study selection
sec.p: A systematic search of electronic databases yielded 662 records from PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane Central. After removing duplicates, 350 records were screened by title and abstract. Of these, 333 were excluded, and 17 full-text articles were sought for retrieval. Three of these articles could not be retrieved; therefore, 14 articles were assessed for eligibility. Twelve studies met the inclusion criteria, and two were excluded (one editorial and one review). Separately, a search of Google Scholar yielded 200 records. After screening, 80 were duplicates, 30 were not retrievable, and the remaining 90 were excluded as they were editorials, reviews, or non-randomized controlled trials. In total, twelve randomized controlled trials were included in the review, and all 12 reports were used for analysis. The study selection process is summarized in the PRISMA 2020 flow diagram (Fig. 1).

sec.title: Study characteristics
sec.p: A total of twelve randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included, involving 99,261 participants with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Five trials evaluated SGLT2 inhibitors (EMPA-REG OUTCOME [3], CANVAS Program [12], DECLARE–TIMI 58 [4], CREDENCE [11], and VERTIS CV [5]), and seven trials evaluated GLP-1 receptor agonists (LEADER [6], SUSTAIN-6 [7], REWIND [8], PIONEER-6 [9], HARMONY [10], FLOW [13], and AMPLITUDE-O [14]). All included studies were multicenter, double-blind RCTs that enrolled adults with established cardiovascular disease or at high risk for it. The mean follow-up duration ranged from 1.6 to 5.4 years.

sec.title: Primary outcome: Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE)

list-item.p: SGLT2 inhibitors vs. placebo: The pooled analysis of five trials showed a significant reduction in MACE (HR = 0.89; 95% CI 0.84–0.95; p = 0.0003), with low heterogeneity (I² = 7%; p = 0.37) (Fig. 2).

caption.p: Forest plot of the meta-analysis for Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE): SGLT2 inhibitors versus placebo

list-item.p: GLP-1 receptor agonists vs. placebo: The pooled analysis of seven trials also showed a significant reduction in MACE (HR = 0.82; 95% CI 0.78–0.87; p < 0.00001), with no heterogeneity (I² = 0%; p = 0.43) (Fig. 3).

caption.p: Forest plot of the meta-analysis for Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE): GLP-1 receptor agonists versus placebo

list-item.p: Indirect comparison: An indirect treatment comparison using the Bucher method indicated that GLP-1 receptor agonists were associated with a nominally greater reduction in MACE compared to SGLT2 inhibitors (HR = 1.09; 95% CI 1.00–1.18; p = 0.0497) (Fig. 4).

caption.p: Result of the indirect treatment comparison for Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE): SGLT2 inhibitors versus GLP-1 receptor agonists

sec.title: Secondary outcomes
sec.p: 1. Hospitalization for Heart Failure (HHF).

list-item.p: SGLT2 inhibitors vs. placebo: A significant reduction was observed (HR = 0.68; 95% CI 0.61–0.76; p < 0.00001) with no heterogeneity (I² = 0%; p = 0.85) (Fig. 5). In the broader literature, this is consistent with meta-analyses on foundational HF pharmacotherapy, where SGLT2i are a key pillar and emerging GLP-1RA data suggest complementary mortality reductions [22].

caption.p: Forest plot of the meta-analysis for Hospitalization for Heart Failure (HHF): SGLT2 inhibitors versus placebo

list-item.p: GLP-1 receptor agonists vs. placebo: A more modest but significant reduction was observed (HR = 0.88; 95% CI 0.80–0.96; p = 0.006), with no heterogeneity (I² = 0%; p = 0.77) (Fig. 6).

caption.p: Forest plot of the meta-analysis for Hospitalization for Heart Failure (HHF): GLP-1 receptor agonists versus placebo

sec.p: 2. Cardiovascular Death.

list-item.p: SGLT2 inhibitors vs. placebo: A significant reduction was observed (HR = 0.83; 95% CI 0.71–0.97; p = 0.02), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 65%; p = 0.02) (Fig. 7).

caption.p: Forest plot of the meta-analysis for Cardiovascular (CV) Death: SGLT2 inhibitors versus placebo

list-item.p: GLP-1 receptor agonists vs. placebo: A significant reduction was observed (HR = 0.87; 95% CI 0.78–0.98; p = 0.02), with no heterogeneity (I² = 0%; p = 0.58) (Fig. 8).

caption.p: Forest plot of the meta-analysis for Cardiovascular (CV) Death: GLP-1 receptor agonists versus placebo

sec.p: 3. All-cause Mortality.

list-item.p: SGLT2 inhibitors vs. placebo: A significant reduction was observed (HR = 0.84; 95% CI 0.75–0.95; p = 0.004), with moderate heterogeneity (I² = 57%; p = 0.05) (Fig. 9).

caption.p: Forest plot of the meta-analysis for All-cause Mortality: SGLT2 inhibitors versus placebo

list-item.p: GLP-1 receptor agonists vs. placebo: A significant reduction was observed (HR = 0.88; 95% CI 0.83–0.95; p = 0.0003), with no heterogeneity (I² = 0%; p = 0.67) (Fig. 10).

caption.p: Forest plot of the meta-analysis for All-cause Mortality: GLP-1 receptor agonists versus placebo

sec.p: 4. Composite Renal Outcome.

list-item.p: SGLT2 inhibitors vs. placebo: A significant reduction was observed (HR = 0.69; 95% CI 0.62–0.77; p < 0.00001), with moderate heterogeneity (I² = 49%; p = 0.10) (Fig. 11). In the broader literature, this aligns with network meta-analyses showing SGLT2i superiority over GLP-1RA for renal endpoints in T2DM, with no significant difference in overall CV mortality [23].

caption.p: Forest plot of the meta-analysis for the Composite Renal Outcome: SGLT2 inhibitors versus placebo

list-item.p: GLP-1 receptor agonists vs. placebo: A significant reduction was observed (HR = 0.76; 95% CI 0.69–0.84; p < 0.00001), with moderate heterogeneity (I² = 47%; p = 0.11) (Fig. 12).

caption.p: Forest plot of the meta-analysis for the Composite Renal Outcome: GLP-1 receptor agonists versus placebo

sec.title: Certainty of the evidence
sec.p: The certainty of the evidence, assessed using the GRADE framework, was high for the reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events with both SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists compared with placebo. This high rating is based on consistent results from randomized trials with a low risk of bias, negligible statistical heterogeneity, direct applicability, precise effect estimates, and no suspected publication bias (Table 2).

caption.p: GRADE evidence profile: major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)

sec.title: Risk of bias assessment
sec.p: The methodological quality of the included randomized controlled trials was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB 1) tool across seven domains: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other bias.

All twelve trials demonstrated a low risk of bias in the core domains critical for internal validity: blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias), blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias) through independent adjudication committees, analysis using intention-to-treat principles (addressing incomplete outcome data), and pre-specification of outcomes (selective reporting bias). For the domain of random sequence generation, five trials (Cannon 2020 [VERTIS], Neal 2017 [CANVAS], Perkovic 2019 [CREDENCE], Perkovic 2024 [FLOW], and Zinman 2015 [EMPA-REG]) were judged as low risk due to explicit description of computer-generated methods; for the remaining seven, the specific method was not detailed, resulting in an unclear risk rating. Similarly, allocation concealment was judged as low risk in four trials (Neal 2017 [CANVAS], Perkovic 2024 [FLOW], Wiviott 2019 [DECLARE], and Zinman 2015 [EMPA-REG]) that described a central interactive system, and unclear risk in eight others. Due to industry sponsorship and involvement in trial design or analysis, the domain of “other bias” was rated as unclear risk for eleven trials; the DECLARE-TIMI 58 trial (Wiviott 2019) was rated low risk in this domain due to independent academic ownership and analysis of the trial data.

Overall, the included trials were judged to have a low to low/unclear risk of bias, supporting the robustness of the evidence synthesized in this meta-analysis. A summary of the risk of bias assessments for each trial is presented in Fig. 13.

caption.p: Summary of the risk of bias assessment for the included randomized controlled trials. Judgements for each domain of the Cochrane Risk of Bias (RoB 1) tool are presented for each individual study. Green indicates low risk of bias, empty box indicates unclear risk, and red indicates high risk of bias

sec.title: Sensitivity analyses
sec.p: To assess the robustness of our primary MACE findings, we performed pre-specified sensitivity analyses. For SGLT2 inhibitors, excluding the trial with a primary renal endpoint (CREDENCE) yielded a consistent hazard ratio (HR = 0.90; 95% CI 0.84–0.97; p = 0.007; I² = 21%) (Fig. 14). For GLP-1 receptor agonists, we conducted two sensitivity analyses: first, excluding the trial that enrolled a uniquely high-risk population (AMPLITUDE-O) (HR = 0.83; 95% CI 0.78–0.88; p < 0.00001; I² = 0%); and second, additionally excluding the renal-outcome trial FLOW (HR = 0.84; 95% CI 0.79–0.90; p < 0.00001; I² = 0%) (Fig. 15). All sensitivity analyses confirmed that the cardioprotective effects of both drug classes remain statistically significant and quantitatively similar to the main analysis, indicating robustness across different trial designs and patient risk profiles (Table 3).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This meta-analysis of 12 randomized controlled trials involving 99,261 high-risk patients with type 2 diabetes presents a comprehensive and up-to-date side-by-side analysis of the cardiovascular and renal safety and efficacy profiles of SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists. Our data confirms that these classes have significant cardioprotective effects compared with placebo but offer differing risk and benefit profiles.

sec.title: Primary outcome and comparative efficacy
sec.p: Pooled analyses have upheld significant decreases in MACE for SGLT2 inhibitors (HR 0.89) and GLP-1 receptor agonists (HR 0.82), with high certainty as per GRADE guidelines. Conversely, defying the hypothesis of drug equality, our methodologically validated indirect analysis employing the Bucher method suggested a nominal superior outcome for GLP-1 receptor agonists with regards to MACE reduction compared with SGLT2 inhibitors (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.00-1.18; p = 0.0497). Although suggesting a potentially divergent class effect based on the point estimate, with bounds reaching unity and thus warranting careful interpretation, it marks a transition from discussions based on equity to more subtle interpretations based on comparative efficacy within the broader perspective of divergent secondary efficacy profiles. Nonetheless, these data are consistent with aggregate meta-analyses indicating the salutary effects on cardiovascular endpoints for these drug classes [1–20].

sec.title: Distinct and complementary outcome profiles
sec.p: The most clinically salient finding of this analysis is the clear divergence in secondary outcomes, which is critical for therapy selection. SGLT2 inhibitors demonstrated a pronounced advantage in reducing hospitalization for heart failure (HR 0.68) and the composite renal outcome (HR 0.69), effects that are both statistically strong and consistent with their primary hemodynamic and metabolic actions [3, 4, 11, 12]. The substantial heterogeneity observed for cardiovascular death with SGLT2 inhibitors (I² = 65%) was largely attributable to the marked effect size in the EMPA-REG OUTCOME trial, a recognized finding in the literature. Conversely, GLP-1 receptor agonists provided more modest but significant benefits on heart failure hospitalizations (HR 0.88) and renal outcomes (HR 0.76), while showing more uniform effects on cardiovascular and all-cause mortality with minimal heterogeneity. Furthermore, GLP-1 receptor agonists are distinguished by their well-established efficacy in reducing atherosclerotic events, such as stroke, and promoting significant weight loss, benefits not shared to the same degree by SGLT2 inhibitors [6–10].

sec.title: Mechanistic insights and pleiotropic effects
sec.p: The complementary cardioprotective profiles are underpinned by differing primary mechanisms: hemodynamic and metabolic effects for SGLT2 inhibitors versus anti-inflammatory and anti-atherogenic pathways for GLP-1 receptor agonists [12–14]. Emerging evidence suggests the benefits of SGLT2 inhibition may extend beyond these primary mechanisms to include potentially important pleiotropic effects. Recent analyses indicate these agents may confer anti-arrhythmic benefits, including a reduction in sudden cardiac death risk [24], and improve endothelial function and cardiac remodeling, as observed in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy [25]. This supports a broader, multifactorial mechanism of cardiovascular protection, further distinguishing their therapeutic niche.

sec.title: Clinical implications and contextual considerations
sec.p: These findings fully align with current guidelines suggesting either class for lowering cardiovascular risk in people with type 2 diabetes and established or high-risk cardiovascular disease [17, 20]. The two classes can be preferentially selected depending on comorbidity risk profiles: SGLT2 inhibitors for people with risk of or with heart failure and kidney disease vs. GLP-1 receptor agonists for people with predominant risk of atherosclerotic CVD and obesity. The sensitivity analyses have also shown robust consistency with MACE endpoints on variable trial designs. A recent meta-analysis supports that benefits with GLP-1 receptor agonists remain consistent with or without SGLT-2 inhibitors, thus recommending combination therapies for people with maximal cardiorenal risk [26].

Written from an Sudanese perspective, it tempers with the challenges made more clear by drug accessibility and affordability challenges within developing nations, as within Sudanese society itself, where healthcare services are objected and intermittent [18–20]. It would be integral, then, within developing nations, to prioritize and develop models founded on evidence. The additional benefits an SGLT2 inhibitor drug may offer unlock a potentially attractive and cost-saving approach, within healthcare systems which might have no option but to choose an initial drug of choice. A 2025 meta-analysis also agreed that SGLT2i significantly reduces risks of HF and all-cause deaths [27].

sec.title: Strengths and limitations
sec.p: Key strengths of this analysis include the use of only high-quality RCTs, a pre-registered protocol, comprehensive sensitivity and GRADE assessments, and a methodologically sound indirect comparison. Limitations include the inherent assumptions of the indirect comparison, heterogeneity in follow-up durations and specific trial populations, and the inability to perform patient-level subgroup analyses to explore treatment-effect modifiers more deeply.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Therefore, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists are highly efficient at preventing major cardiovascular outcomes in high-risk type 2 diabetes, with a nominally larger difference seen with GLP-1 receptor agonists. Their distinctly different risk/benefit profile for HF, kidney protection, atherosclerosis events, and weight reduction supports the fact that these classes are not equivalent but complementary. Personalized treatment should be recommended based on comorbidities and facilities, as mentioned above, to maximize the large cardiorenal effects associated with these classes. Recent data from meta-analyses on combination treatment have demonstrated additive effects on cardiorenal benefits, offering more clues on treatment options for comorbidity patients [28].
